1023.title: The teacher nearby
1023.hook: the most important teacher may be at a local temple
1023.howItsDone: Buddhists in Asia often learn at the neighborhood temple, where resident monks or nuns teach and lead ceremonies; elsewhere, local sitting groups led by monastics or trained lay teachers meet weekly and welcome newcomers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Therigatha, Soma under her tree, and women leading in the halls today. Your line: they lead.

A row of shoes by a door in a strip mall, between a laundromat and a tax office. Inside, a small room: a Buddha on a shelf, cushions, a kettle, and a monk or a lay teacher who's been there every week for years, sitting with whoever turns up. No livestream, no book tour. For weeks now, this path has walked with famous names: Dogen, Hakuin, Ajahn Chah, the Dalai Lama. Today turns toward the door you may have walked past without noticing.
screen: `SHOES BY A STRIP-MALL DOOR.` → `FAMOUS NAMES FOR WEEKS.` → `NOW, THE DOOR NEARBY.`

segments.voice: There's a short exchange in the Pali Canon. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, comes to him with a thought he's been turning over. Admirable friendship, he says, having good companions on the path, must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrects him. Don't say that, Ananda. Admirable friendship is the whole of the holy life. The Pali word is kalyanamitta, a lovely friend, a good friend in the dharma. Notice the kind of teacher this points to. Not someone you admire from far away. A friend: someone who knows your face, sees you on a bad week, notices when you stop coming. Books and recorded talks can teach a great deal, and famous teachers have real gifts. But a book can't see you slump on the cushion. A recording can't ask how your mother is doing. The person at the local temple or sitting group can. Where Buddhism is old, the local temple can be where people learn: the monk down the road who chants at a funeral, teaches children, listens to a farmer's worry. Elsewhere, the nearby teacher might be a lay volunteer who opens a room on Tuesday nights. Traditions differ in how they choose and train teachers, and some places nearby will suit you better than others. That's fine. The point of the old exchange is simple: the path is walked with people, and the ones who can walk it with you are close enough to know you. Some readers take a plain lesson from it: look first for the good friend nearby.
screen: `HALF THE HOLY LIFE? NO, THE WHOLE.` · `KALYANAMITTA: A GOOD FRIEND.` · `A BOOK CAN'T SEE YOU SLUMP.` · `THE TEMPLE DOWN THE ROAD.` · then, large: `CLOSE ENOUGH TO KNOW YOU.`

segments.voice: Picture the streets around where you live, slowly, as if you were walking them: is there a temple, a meditation group, a quiet room where people sit together? You may not know, and that's fine; just notice the not knowing. Then remember someone close by who has already been a good friend to your practice, even without the title of teacher, and let a little thanks go toward them.
Kalyanamitta. The good friend close enough to know you, whom the Buddha called the whole of the holy life.
Your line: nearby. Good friendship is the whole of the path, not half. See you tomorrow.

1024.title: How teachers fail
1024.hook: some teachers have abused trust; the tradition's own rules exist to guard against it
1024.howItsDone: Monastic communities recite the Vinaya rules together and confess offenses, and some Buddhist organizations now publish ethics guidelines and grievance procedures for teachers, encouraging students to raise concerns openly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kalyanamitta, the good friend close enough to know you. Your line: nearby.

Here's a strange instruction from the Buddha's own mouth, as the Pali Canon tells it. He tells his monks to investigate him. Not to take his word that he's awakened, but to watch what he does over time: is his conduct clean, is anything hidden, has fame changed him? The teacher hands the students the tools to check the teacher. Today is about why that matters, because teachers can fail.
screen: `THE BUDDHA SAYS: INVESTIGATE ME.` → `WATCH THE CONDUCT, OVER TIME.` → `TEACHERS CAN FAIL.`

segments.voice: Start with the hard fact. In our own time, some Buddhist teachers, in Asia and in the West, monks and laypeople, have abused the trust of their students: sexually, financially, or by controlling their lives. Their communities and students have said so publicly, and some organizations have changed their rules because of it. That's painful to hear on a path about kindness. But the tradition saw this danger early. In the monastic code, the Vinaya, rules come with stories: a monk did something that caused harm, and the Buddha said, from now on, not this. Monks and nuns gather regularly to recite those rules aloud, and to confess where they've broken them. The guardrails were built in. Then there's the teaching to the Kalamas, people confused by teachers who each praised their own way. The Buddha tells them not to go by tradition, or by a teacher's reputation, or because this one is our teacher. When you know for yourselves that something leads to harm and suffering, he says, let it go. And there's the instruction from the hook, in the sutta about the inquirer: check even the Buddha by his conduct. In Tibetan Buddhism, where devotion to a teacher runs deep, the tradition also advises that a student examine a teacher carefully, for a long time, before taking them on. So here are warning signs the tradition itself would recognize: a teacher who can't be questioned; secrecy; demands for money, sex or total obedience; being told to cut off the people who love you. Trust is part of practice. Checking is part of it too.
screen: `SOME TEACHERS HAVE ABUSED TRUST.` · `THE VINAYA: RULES BUILT FROM HARM.` · `THE KALAMAS: KNOW FOR YOURSELVES.` · `WARNING SIGNS THE TRADITION KNOWS.` · then, large: `CHECK EVEN THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: Let the warning signs come back slowly, and choose the one that stands out to you; hold it calmly, the way you'd remember where the fire exit is. This isn't suspicion of anyone in particular; it's knowing the exit, so you can rest in the room. If any of this touches something in your own life, it's wise to talk to someone you trust outside the group.
Vimamsaka. The inquirer, the title of the sutta where the Buddha tells monks to investigate even him, a guard against abuse of trust.
Your line: trust, but check. Even the Buddha asked to be checked. Day one thousand twenty-four.

1025.title: Why lineage matters
1025.hook: teaching passed person to person, checked and handed on
1025.howItsDone: Zen communities chant the names of their lineage ancestors, Tibetan teachers give reading transmissions and empowerments received from their own teachers, and monastic ordinations are conferred by monks or nuns who already hold them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vimamsaka, the Buddha telling his monks to investigate even him. Your line: trust, but check.

Who taught the person who taught you to ride a bike? The answer may be a blank. But in a Zen hall, at certain ceremonies, people chant a long list of names: teacher, and teacher's teacher, back and back, until the list reaches the Buddha. In a Tibetan monastery, before a text is studied, a teacher may read it aloud so the students receive it the way the teacher once received it. A family tree, but of teaching. Why would anyone bother keeping it?
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOUR TEACHER?` → `A CHANTED LIST OF NAMES.` → `A FAMILY TREE OF TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Lineage means the chain of people a teaching has passed through. In the Pali Canon, as the Buddha is dying, he tells Ananda not to think the disciples will be left without a teacher: the Dhamma and the discipline he taught will be their teacher after he is gone. So the teaching itself is the center. But it has to be carried, and people carry it. Monastic ordination, as the day on the nuns showed, is handed on by those who already hold it. A Zen teacher receives permission to teach from their own teacher, who checks their understanding first. Tibetan teachers speak of receiving a transmission, a reading or an empowerment, from someone who received it before them. Why keep track? Partly quality control: a teaching tested by a teacher who was tested by a teacher has been checked again and again. Partly honesty: you can say where your teaching came from. And partly gratitude: the names in the chant are people who kept the lamp lit. But here's the balance, and it comes from the Buddha too. In his talk to the Kalamas, one thing he tells them not to rely on alone is parampara, the chain of tradition handed down. A lineage on its own doesn't prove a teacher is good, as yesterday made clear. It gives you a way to check; the conduct is still the test. Schools weigh lineage differently; some put it at the center, some keep it quietly in the background. Either way, the names are kept.
screen: `THE DHAMMA WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.` · `CARRIED PERSON TO PERSON.` · `CHECKED, HONEST, GRATEFUL.` · `PARAMPARA: NOT PROOF ON ITS OWN.` · then, large: `HANDED ON.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you something that matters, a skill, a way of being, a kind of patience, and then step back one link to whoever taught them, even if you don't know their name. Step back once more, if you can, and picture that person however dimly. Let a little thanks run back along the chain, link by link, to people you'll never meet.
Parampara. The chain of teachers handed down person to person, checked along the way, and honored, though never proof on its own.
Your line: handed on. The teaching is the teacher; people carry it. Day one thousand twenty-five, done.

1026.title: Poets and painters
1026.hook: Sengai's circle-triangle-square, Ryokan's poems, thangka painters
1026.howItsDone: In Zen, monks and lay students practice brush painting and calligraphy, including the ink circle; in Tibetan Buddhism, thangka painters train with a master for years, follow set proportions, and paintings are consecrated before use in shrines and meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parampara, a chain of teachers chanted back to the Buddha. Your line: handed on.

Three shapes in black ink: a circle, a triangle and a square, overlapping, drawn quickly with a wet brush. Beside them, a short line of writing that names the painter's temple and explains nothing. The Zen monk Sengai painted it in Japan, and people still argue about what it means. Some see the whole universe in it. Some see the schools of Buddhism. Some just see a monk having fun with a brush.
screen: `A CIRCLE, A TRIANGLE, A SQUARE.` → `NOTHING EXPLAINED.` → `TEACHING WITH INK.`

segments.voice: Sengai was a Zen abbot who painted loose, funny, warm pictures: frogs sitting in meditation, monks laughing, plain shapes. He left no explanation of his circle, triangle and square, and that silence may be the teaching: the picture doesn't hand you an answer, it hands you a question to sit with, the way a koan does. Then Ryokan, the poet-monk this path met earlier, playing with children and pitying a thief. He wrote short poems in plain words about his begging rounds, rain on his hut, an empty bowl, falling leaves. Nothing grand. The practice is in the attention: he notices small things so fully that the poem feels like a sitting written down. Then go west, to the Himalayas, to the thangka painters of Tibet. A thangka is a painting on cloth, usually of a buddha, a bodhisattva or a mandala, made to be used in practice: hung in a shrine, looked at in meditation. Here there's no loose brushwork. The painter follows careful grids and set proportions, handed down from teacher to student, so every line is in its place. Some painters recite and keep vows while they work, and the finished painting may be consecrated before it's hung. Three very different ways to make art as practice: Sengai's playful ink, Ryokan's plain words, the thangka painter's exact lines. One loose, one quiet, one precise. What they share is attention, poured into the brush or the word until the work itself becomes a kind of sitting.
screen: `SENGAI: A PUZZLE WITH NO ANSWER.` · `RYOKAN: PLAIN WORDS, FULL ATTENTION.` · `THANGKA: EXACT LINES, HANDED DOWN.` · `LOOSE, QUIET, PRECISE.` · then, large: `THE WORK BECOMES A SITTING.`

segments.voice: With any pen and scrap of paper, or a finger on your palm, draw a single circle slowly, paying attention to the whole movement: the start, the curve, where it closes or doesn't. Don't fix it; look at it, and if there's time, add a triangle, then a square, each one its own small sitting. It doesn't have to be good, only done with attention.
Enso. The Zen ink circle Sengai drew, alongside Ryokan's plain poems and the thangka painter's exact lines: teachers whose art was practice.
Your line: practice in art. Loose, quiet or precise, the attention is the same. That's day one thousand twenty-six.

1027.title: Unknown teachers
1027.hook: the grandmothers, lay chanters and village monks no one wrote down
1027.howItsDone: In many Buddhist homes and temples, people remember parents, elders and teachers when they make offerings or dedicate merit, and some temples hold days of gratitude for teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: enso, Sengai's circle, triangle and square, Ryokan's poems, a thangka painter's patient brush. Your line: practice in art.

A certain monk. A certain nun. A certain lay follower. Some of the old discourses open that way, with no name at all. Someone walked a long road, sat down in front of the Buddha, asked the question keeping them up at night, and the text keeps the question and lets the name go. Somebody's grandmother lit the lamp before dawn and taught a small child to put her palms together. A farmer chanted the refuges at a funeral because he knew the words. A village monk, never famous, answered the same question kindly, again and again. Today is for them.
screen: `THE QUESTION KEPT, THE NAME LET GO.`
`THE GRANDMOTHER, THE FARMER, THE VILLAGE MONK.`

segments.voice: Start with the Buddha's last months, in the long discourse on his final passing. Years earlier, the text says, Mara, the tempter, came and urged him to pass away at once: his work was done. The Buddha refused. He would not go until his monks and nuns, and his lay followers, men and women both, had learned the teaching well enough to live it and explain it to others. Notice who's on that list. Not only the robed. The householder with a shop and children counts too. In this telling, the teaching was meant from the beginning to travel in ordinary hands. Now the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. Its poems carry the names of the women who spoke them, and at least one is credited simply to a certain nun, whose words were kept and whose name was not. Then a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya about two kinds of people hard to find in the world: the one who does a kindness first, without being asked, and the one who knows what was done for them and is grateful. The Pali word for that second quality is kataññuta, knowing what was done. Put those together and you get today's idea. Behind the names in this year's story, Nagarjuna, Milarepa, Dogen, Ajahn Chah, stood people no one wrote down: the one who first taught them to bow, to sit, to chant a line. The texts are honest about it. They leave the blank.
screen: `MARA SAYS GO. THE BUDDHA SAYS NOT YET.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who taught you something real and will never be in a book: a neighbor, a coach, a grandparent, the person who showed you how to apologize. Let their face come, or their voice, or just their hands doing something, and let the thanks be there quietly, the way you'd hold a cup of tea for someone. If they've died, the thanks still counts.
Unknown teachers. The grandmothers, chanters and village monks who carried the teaching hand to hand, and whose names the books let go.
Your line: no one wrote them down. The names were lost; the teaching still arrived. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

1028.title: Your teachers
1028.hook: the people who taught you anything true
1028.howItsDone: Buddhists in many places honor teachers with bows, offerings and gratitude ceremonies, and the advice to Sigala is taught in some communities as a guide to everyday relationships, teachers among them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: unknown teachers, the grandmothers, chanters and village monks the books let go. Your line: no one wrote them down.

A note in red pen in the margin of an old school essay: good, now say what you mean. A coach's voice from the sideline, repeating the same two words all season. An aunt in a kitchen, measuring salt by the look of it, not the spoon. Some teachers have titles. Some have none: a coworker, a kid down the street, a stranger on a long bus ride who told the truth when a polite lie would have been easier. Today turns the lamp toward the teachers in a life like yours.

Today's text is the Buddha's advice to a young householder named Sigala. As the story goes, Sigala's dying father told him to honor the directions, so each morning Sigala bows to the east, south, west, north, the sky and the earth. The Buddha gives the old custom a new meaning. The directions, he says, are the people in your life: parents, teachers, a spouse and children, friends, workers, and religious teachers. Honor them by how you treat them. The teachers are the south. A student looks after a teacher by rising to greet them, attending on them, wanting to learn, listening closely. Then the text turns around: a teacher owes the student good training, makes sure they've really grasped what was taught, and speaks well of them to friends. So a teacher isn't a vending machine for facts. A teacher keeps an eye on you, checks you understood, and is proud of you in public. The same discourse describes a true friend who sounds a lot like a teacher: the friend who gives good counsel. That friend keeps you from wrong, encourages you in what is good, tells you what you hadn't heard before, and shows you the way to heaven. No robe is mentioned. Learning here happens in households and friendships, not only temples. A teacher might be the monk at the local vihara. It might be the friend who drove you to the hospital, or the boss who corrected you without shaming you. The text doesn't call every friend a teacher. It describes what the good ones do.
screen: `STUDENT AND TEACHER LOOK AFTER EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Let three people come to mind who taught you something true; not the most important three, just three. For each, find the single thing they taught you in a few plain words, like she taught me to finish what I start, and hold it for a few breaths before moving on. If someone difficult shows up on the list, that's allowed; hard teachers count too.
Your teachers. The people who taught you anything true, with or without a title. In the advice to Sigala, they're a direction worth bowing to.
Your line: proud of you in public. That's what the good ones do. See you tomorrow.

1029.title: Becoming a teacher
1029.hook: the Buddha sends his monks out to wander, and a stranger learns from the way one of them walks
1029.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, monastics are expected to teach through conduct as well as words, and many lay Buddhists speak of practice at home and work as the way they pass the teaching on.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your teachers, Sigala bowing to the directions, and the teacher who checks you understood. Your line: proud of you in public.

A monk named Assaji is walking through the city of Rajagaha on his alms round, bowl in hand. He isn't preaching. He isn't saying anything at all. A young wanderer named Sariputta, a pupil of another teacher who is still searching for the deathless, sees him and stops. Something in the way this monk moves, going forward, looking back, eyes down, calm, makes Sariputta follow him down the street. When the round is done, he asks: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji says he's new, and can only say a little. A little turns out to be enough.

That scene comes from the Vinaya, the book of the monastic discipline. A little earlier in the same book, the Buddha has a small group of monks who have understood the teaching, sixty, the text says, and he sends them out. Go and wander, he tells them, for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world. And don't let two of you take the same road. So teaching begins as walking: roads, villages, alms rounds, not lecture halls. And the Assaji story shows what that can look like: a person whose way of moving made someone else curious. The lesson started before a word was spoken. The Dhammapada puts the order plainly. In Max Muller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer." Yourself first, then others; the verse doesn't let the second step come before the first. This week looked at teachers near and far, famous and forgotten. Today the arrow turns toward the listener. In this picture, nobody needs a title to teach. Someone who practices is often being watched by someone else: a child, a roommate, a coworker who notices how they handle a bad morning. Becoming a teacher, here, is less a decision than something that happens when practice shows.
screen: `GO AND WANDER, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, upright and easy, the way Assaji might have walked: not stiff, not showing off. Bring to mind one person who will see you today, and pick one small thing you'd want them to catch from you without being told: patience in a line, putting the phone down when they talk, a real thank-you. Don't plan a speech; just let that one thing be the lesson.
Carika. The wandering the Buddha sent his monks on, so that the way they moved taught before they spoke.
Your line: by example. Yourself first, then others, as the verse says. Day one thousand twenty-nine, done.
